title: Real AI Agents Need Planning, Not Just Prompting - Yuval Belfer

primary.label: Agent Architecture & Harnesses
primary.rationale: Selected by Jev (System One, jev-1.13.0) from the 17-category taxonomy using the talk's summary, takeaways, concepts and technologies (confidence 100%).

domains.label: General Purpose
domains.rationale: The talk centers on agent loop design, planning architecture, dynamic replanning, and execution engine harnesses with AI21 Maestro as the exemplar system. The planning and execution engine concepts are domain-agnostic and applicable across agent use cases. The talk presents agent architecture design and includes benchmark evaluation of the Maestro system. Prerequisites include basic LLM familiarity and understanding of agent frameworks like ReAct and function calling. The content is a conference presentation delivered at the AI Engineer channel. Multiple transcript evidence anchors directly support the agent architecture classification with consistent thematic coverage.

summary: Yuval Belfer (AI21 Labs) opens by tracing the instruction-following problem from InstructGPT (2022) to GPT 4.1 (2025), noting that all LLMs still struggle to follow complex instructions. He attributes this to the modern practice of cramming all context, constraints, and requirements into a single prompt and hoping for the best, arguing that LLMs alone are insufficient even for supposedly simple tasks like instruction following. He surveys common agent paradigms—LLM routing, function calling, MCP-based tool integration, and ReAct—dismissing philosophical debates about what qualifies as an agent in favor of pragmatism. He specifically critiques ReAct for operating step-by-step without any look-ahead to the overall plan, making it unsuitable for complex tasks requiring parallelization and explainability. Belfer defines planning as figuring out the steps needed to reach a goal, applicable when problems lack straightforward solutions. He introduces dynamic planning, which allows mid-execution replanning, and emphasizes that every planner needs a smart execution engine to analyze inter-step dependencies, enable parallel execution, and balance speed versus cost (e.g., via branch prediction). He then presents AI21 Maestro, which separates context, task, and requirements for easier validation, uses an execution tree where the planner and engine generate multiple candidates, pursue the most promising ones within a predefined budget, and iteratively fix and validate. Techniques include best-of-n sampling at high temperature (or using different LLMs), discarding weak candidates, and a final reduce step combining results. Benchmark results show Maestro significantly improving GPT-4o, Claude Sonnet 3.5, and o3-mini on instruction-following and an internal requirement-satisfaction dataset, at the cost of more runtime and money. Belfer concludes with a pragmatic escalation ladder: start simple with SLMs, then tool-augmented models, then ReAct, and only adopt full planning plus execution engines for genuinely complex tasks.
whyItMatters: The talk connects its engineering abstractions, implementation choices, and AI/product implications into one practical system view.

sections.title: The Instruction-Following Problem
sections.summary: Belfer traces instruction following from InstructGPT (2022) to GPT 4.1 (2025), noting all LLMs still struggle. He attributes this to developers cramming all context, constraints, and requirements into a single prompt, arguing LLMs alone are no longer enough even for simple tasks.

sections.title: What Is an Agent? Survey of Paradigms
sections.summary: Belfer surveys common agent definitions—LLM routing, function calling, MCP-based tool integration, and ReAct—dismissing philosophical debates in favor of pragmatism. He introduces himself as working at AI21 Labs on language models and an agentic framework.

sections.title: ReAct Limitations and the Case for Planning
sections.summary: Belfer critiques ReAct for operating step-by-step without look-ahead to the overall plan. He defines planning as figuring out steps to reach a goal, needed for complex tasks requiring parallelization and explainability. He mentions forms-based planners (Magentic-One) and code-based planners.

sections.title: Dynamic Planning and Smart Execution
sections.summary: Belfer introduces dynamic planning with mid-execution replanning and the need for a smart execution engine that analyzes step dependencies, enables parallel execution, and balances speed versus cost via techniques like branch prediction.

sections.title: AI21 Maestro: Architecture and Techniques
sections.summary: Belfer presents AI21 Maestro, which separates context, task, and requirements for easier validation. The planner and execution engine generate multiple candidates, pursue the most promising within a predefined budget, and iteratively fix and validate. Techniques include best-of-n sampling at high temperature, discarding weak candidates, and a final reduce step. A more complex example shows expected cost, latency, and success probability guiding path selection.

sections.title: Benchmarks and Results
sections.summary: Belfer shows Maestro significantly improving GPT-4o, Claude 3.5 Sonnet, and o3-mini on instruction-following benchmarks and an internal requirement-satisfaction dataset, trading more runtime and money for higher quality.

sections.title: Takeaways and Conclusion
sections.summary: Belfer concludes with a pragmatic escalation ladder: start simple with SLMs, then tool-augmented models, then ReAct, and adopt full planning plus execution engines only for genuinely complex tasks. He invites attendees to join the Maestro waitlist.
